newsitem.title: ZAIRE: World focus on refugee plight, Zaire battles rage.
newsitem.headline: World focus on refugee plight, Zaire battles rage.

text.p: International relief agencies and policy planners focused on the plight of more than one million Hutu refugees in embattled eastern Zaire, with protected "humanitarian corridors" the favoured option.

Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, said in Geneva that "emergency lifelines" should be opened to help the refugees and displaced Zaireans alike, with corridors for the Hutus to return in safety to their homes in Rwanda and Burundi.

But as fighting between Tutsi rebels and Zairean troops raged on within earshot of Bukavu and around the main city of Goma, aid workers said refugees had begun to move west from the world's largest refugee camp at Mugunga and deeper into Zaire.
In Brussels, the European Union said a ceasefire had first to be declared before the flood of refugees caught in the cross-border conflict could be helped on a mass scale.
"The essential first requirement is a ceasefire...Only then can we begin the massive humanitarian job that needs to be done," a statement from the EU's Irish presidency said.
"Only then too can we begin addressing the long-standing wider problem of the over one million Rwandan refugees in that area and in the region as a whole," it added.
In a broadcast monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation, Rwandan radio said the Rwandan government said it would help in all international efforts to end the conflict.
But the government statement accused the Kinshasa government and the international community of turning a blind eye to growing problems in the region for the past few months.

"The paradox of the eastern Zaire tragedy is that Kinshasa and the international community have watched with almost total indifference the events as they unfolded over a period of several months," it said.

The statement went on to call on the international community to view the crisis in eastern Zaire as a conflict between the Zairean state and internal forces, rather than as a conflict between two countries.
Many Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 fearing Tutsi reprisals after the genocide of up to a million Tutsis there.
"The further the refugees move west, the more difficult it will be for us to reach them. It may make repatriation and reconciliation impossible," Ogata said in a statement.
Bloody rivalry between majority Hutus and minority Tutsis has poisoned life in Rwanda and Burundi for generations and has now spilled on to the territory of vast, mineral-rich Zaire.
The crisis for Zaire has sharpened with the absence of veteran president Mobutu Sese Seko, receiving treatment for cancer in Switzerland.

Zaire accuses Tutsi-led Rwanda, which has long complained of cross-border raids by Hutu hardliners living among the refugees, of sending troops to fight alongside the rebels. Journalists saw Rwandan troops in Goma on Saturday. Rwanda denies involvement.

Residents saw smoke from four Rwandan refugee camps near the airport to the north of Bukavu on Sunday and said the rebels' main fighters had left for the frontlines. Heavy explosions and firing could be heard for about 90 minutes.
Sporadic gunfire in Goma city centre and around its airport, a key target five km (three miles) to the north, could be heard in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi overnight and on Sunday.
In Kinshasa, Tutsis, leading members of the capital's business and professional community, were packing up and trying to leave after weekend attacks on their homes and property.
Part-Tutsi prime minister, Kengo wa Dondo, accused by the army of not doing enough to help the troops at the front, came under growing pressure to resign.
Kengo's main opposition rivals say they have opened talks with supporters of the ailing Mobutu on forming a government of national unity.

"The two political families, that of Etienne Tshisekedi and that of Mobutu, have established contact and we may very soon see a government of national unity," Tshisekedi spokesman Mukendi wa Mulumba said.

Tshisekedi, elected prime minister by a national conference in 1992 but shunted aside in favour of a Mobutu appointee a year later, has never accepted Kengo's 1994 election by the transitional parliament as a compromise candidate.
Ogata, who is sending her deputy to Rwanda and Zaire, said the Hutu refugees and displaced Zaireans needed urgent help.

France, which has troops stationed near Zaire and provided safe havens after the 1994 Rwanda genocide, said it was considering a European plan for "humanitarian corridors" but said any intervention needed an international or U.N. mandate.
Officials said France was waiting for a signal from African leaders, due to discuss Zaire in Nairobi on Tuesday. The European Union said a truce was a pre-condition for mass aid.
